doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

title: Global Jazz Studies at Brooklyn College and UCLA
summary: He created the Global Jazz Studies program at Brooklyn College and found one at UCLA, arguing jazz is a made-up word and not solely an American invention.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: At UCLA you were, or still are, the professor of Global Jazz Studies. And I wonder if that title, if you were in on that title. Because it’s not a common thing if you look at other colleges and their jazz department, it stands out that you call it “Global Jazz Studies.”

I actually created the Global Jazz Studies program first for Brooklyn College and then when I went to UCLA they already had a Global Jazz Studies program in place. So a lot of that is the realization that a lot of academia is making about the nature of jazz. In the first case we have to — this is not a popular position but I’ll go ahead and state it. Jazz is — we know this, it’s a verifiable fact — jazz is a word that was made up for a concert. It was put on a flyer and it was even denigrated — it was, I forget the exact breakdown but it was a fairly racist trope. Jazz is not an invention, it’s not an American invention, it’s not — jazz is something that was formed here by people of African descent. It’s a very, very tricky position to take because that same — again as I said earlier — that same, those same forces that fomented the creation of black music in the Americas happened wherever black musicians were in the Americas. So to call jazz an American invention is like saying classical music is a Viennese invention, actually the work of many people who come together to bring about a very wide definition of course and the ultimate example is Mozart who was a Viennese-Austrian-German writing Italian-French music. I mean it’s all kind of that thing which is — so in a way jazz is a word that I think people have adopted to nationalize an art form, and to affirm themselves in a way that I think is very unhealthy.
